summary: Garrett Galow, who runs product at WorkOS (an enterprise platform features developer platform powering companies like Cursor, Anthropic, and OpenAI), presents Studio—an internal workspace tool built to break the inefficient cycle of business questions requiring engineering intervention. The traditional loop involves someone asking a question, explaining context, waiting for an engineer to write SQL, discovering the answer needs refinement, and sharing one-off results in Slack that don't scale. Studio connects to Snowflake, Linear, and Notion as data sources. Users ask questions via an internal dashboard or Slack bot, which triggers an API that parses requests and routes them through LangGraph—an agent powered by Claude Opus with tools and a guidance layer. An integration proxy handles data source connections, and Convex stores state across sessions. The key innovation is widgets: sandboxed JavaScript code the LLM generates once, containing the UI, API calls, and queries needed to power a reusable tool. After generation, every subsequent run is deterministic and costs nothing in LLM tokens—the LLM is not involved until someone requests an adjustment. Three engineering decisions made Studio reliable. First, sequencing: the agent runs preflight checks and injects tool-specific schema context only at tool invocation, not upfront, keeping the context window clean. Second, layering: a base prompt with defaults plus org-specific rules per tool, including instructing the LLM to distrust its own knowledge about WorkOS and go to primary sources since the product changes quickly. Third, validation: every generated Snowflake query is run and validated to return data before being hardcoded into a widget, catching the failure mode of valid SQL that returns zero rows. Garrett notes Studio does not use a RAG database—it invokes tools directly with context on top, and LLMs are surprisingly good at interpreting table schemas with descriptive column names. Complex joins (like a four-join customer-to-user mapping) are handled by providing a context block once. For governance, context includes instructions like filtering for non-deleted and active-status entities, which prevents common errors. Data can be combined from multiple tools in a single widget. Currently integrations are per-user, but WorkOS is building org connectors using their own Pipes product, with a permissioning layer for role-based access. Evals run identically in staging and production. On cost, Garrett says they are willing to pay Opus pricing because it outperforms alternatives and quality tradeoff is unacceptable.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & WorkOS Background
sections.summary: Garrett introduces himself as running product at WorkOS, which does enterprise platform features as a developer platform powering Cursor, Anthropic, and OpenAI. He clarifies he will discuss internal tooling, not the product itself.

sections.title: The Problem: Business Question Loop
sections.summary: Describes the repetitive loop where non-technical staff ask business questions, explain context to engineers, wait for SQL answers, discover they need deeper data, and share one-off Slack results that don't scale. Dashboards are too rigid for evolving questions.

sections.title: Studio Overview & Architecture
sections.summary: Introduces Studio as an internal workspace for self-serve questions and app building. Architecture: Slack bot or dashboard triggers an API that parses requests through LangGraph (agent with Opus LLM, tools, guidance layer). Integration proxy connects to Snowflake, Linear, Notion. Convex stores state across sessions.

sections.title: Demo: Content Attribution Widget
sections.summary: Demonstrates asking which content drives most new team sign-ups. Studio queries Snowflake, identifies schemas, and builds a reusable widget with UI, APIs, and queries. The widget shows blog posts, changelogs, and docs effectiveness across time slices with category filters, and re-runs deterministically.

sections.title: Demo: Radar Support Widget
sections.summary: Shows a Radar security lookup widget where support staff search by email to see blocked/unblocked login sessions for customers like Cursor. Support team uses this in Slack for self-service investigations without platform team involvement, and can share recurring widgets internally.

sections.title: Reliability Engineering: Sequencing & Layering
sections.summary: Introduces three reliability pillars. Sequencing: preflight checks for tool connectivity and context, clarifying questions, and just-in-time schema context injection at tool invocation rather than upfront. Layering: base prompt with defaults plus org-specific rules per tool setup. Third pillar (query validation) is introduced but not detailed in this section.

sections.title: Reliability: Distrust, Validation & Evals
sections.summary: Completes the layering pillar by instructing the LLM to distrust its own knowledge about WorkOS and consult primary sources like docs, since the product changes quickly. Details the validation pillar: every Snowflake query is run and checked for returned data before being hardcoded into widgets, catching valid SQL that returns zero rows. Evals run identically in staging and production for consistent experience.

sections.title: Q&A: Data Cleanup, No RAG, Governance
sections.summary: Garrett explains Studio does not require Snowflake data cleanup; complex four-deep joins are handled by telling Studio about them once via context blocks. No RAG database is used—tools are invoked directly with context on top, and LLMs interpret schemas well with descriptive column names. For governance, context includes rules like filtering non-deleted and active-status entities, which prevents common errors; the hit rate is very high and remaining errors are obvious.

sections.title: Q&A: Multi-Tool Data, Widget Reliability, Permissions, Cost
sections.summary: Widgets can combine data from multiple tools via JavaScript making direct API calls. Once created, widgets are deterministic—no LLM involvement until adjustments are requested. User inputs are passed as JavaScript arguments, not parsed by the LLM at runtime. Currently integrations are per-user; WorkOS is building org connectors using their own Pipes product with role-based permissioning. On cost, they accept Opus pricing because it outperforms alternatives and the quality tradeoff is unacceptable.

demonstrations: Content attribution widget: asking which site content leads to most new team sign-ups, with table view across time slices and category filters
Radar security lookup widget: searching for blocked user sessions by email, showing login history with blocked/not-blocked status for a Cursor customer
Live widget re-run showing deterministic query execution against Snowflake for different time slices
limitations: Per-user integrations are currently required for each data source, which is annoying for broad deployment
Per-user login model means some employees lack access to tools like Salesforce they should be able to read
Org connectors with role-based permissioning are still being built, not yet available
